primary_sources: Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898

stimulus.source_note: Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898, public domain.
stimulus.text: "If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did — we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward — we only continue the march of the flag?" — Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim abridged excerpt from Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898, public domain.
stem: Beveridge's argument would most directly support which of the following actions?

options.text: Annexing the Philippines after the Spanish-American War

options.misconception: Refusing annexation is what President Cleveland did. Beveridge's logic points the other way, toward taking territory.

options.text: Withdrawing American Marines from Nicaragua in the 1930s
options.misconception: The 1930s withdrawal was a turn away from intervention. Beveridge argues for stepping forward, not back.

options.text: Rejecting the League of Nations in 1919
options.misconception: The League fight was about joining an international body, not about holding colonies. Beveridge's case is about empire.

rationales.A: Beveridge's continuity argument was made to win the annexation debate: taking the Philippines was just the flag marching on.
rationales.B: Background: Cleveland refused Hawaii in 1893 because most Hawaiians still backed their queen. Beveridge's logic points toward taking territory, not refusing it.
rationales.C: Background: the 1930s withdrawal from Nicaragua was a turn away from intervention. Beveridge argues for stepping forward, not back.
rationales.D: Background: the League fight was about joining an international body. Beveridge's case is about holding colonies, a different question.
rationales.general:
1. Name Beveridge's move. Empire is the flag marching on, so taking new land is normal.
2. Ask which action that move justifies. Annexing the Philippines is the case he was arguing in 1898.
3. Test the rest. Refusing Hawaii, withdrawing Marines, and rejecting the League all run against his direction.
4. Put it together. His argument was built for one vote: whether to keep the Philippines.
Remember: match an argument to the decision it was made for, not to any later decision that sounds similar.
